# Explainers, tutorials and "how it works"

One idea the viewer understands by the end (`../story.md` §1). The spine is one concrete example worked through, start to finish, not a tour of facts. Usually 30–90 s.

## Ground it first

Start where the viewer already is: a person, a place or a situation they know, and a question they would ask about it ("why does the astronaut come home younger than her twin?"). The abstract device (a light clock, a graph, a field) enters inside that situation, as the thing that answers the question, and the film returns to the person at the end with the answer. A film that opens on the device alone is a diagram, not an explainer.

## Devices that explain

- **The object is the explanation.** Build a thing whose working is the idea: a machine, a model, a map, a light clock, drawn so it reads as what it is (its material, its mount, where it sits in the scene). Every number on screen comes from it, and the camera tours through it: cutaways, an exploded view, a dive into the part that matters.
- **One diagram that grows.** Start from the simplest true picture and add one part per beat, each appearing when it is named; never a finished diagram dropped on screen at once.
- **Continuous transformation.** Each step morphs out of the last (a bar becomes an axis, a dot becomes a population), so the viewer never loses the thread to a cut.
- **The worked example.** One real input (a sentence, a number, a photo) travels through every step to the answer.

## Shapes of information

Most explainable lines are one of a few shapes, and each has its own picture: a number that lands (`data.md`); a myth turned over (the wrong idea struck through, the right one printed over it); before and after; many things converging into a few groups; a network that densifies; one chosen out of many; steps in order; a real screenshot with the detail circled; a quote set as a poster; a chapter card. Pick the shape first, then the picture, so similar lines get different pictures and every line gets the one that shows it.

## Words

- Narrated: the voice is the clock (`../sound.md` §2). Reveal each part when the voice names it, across the back half of the scene; keep a scene to about 19 spoken words (`../film.md` "Script and pacing").
- Not narrated: large lines carry it, up to about 10 words, each held 0.5 s + 0.3 s a word.
- Labels sit on the part they name, with a leader line when needed, and appear with it. No legends, no bullet slides.

## Getting it right

- Every claim, value and step traces to the source; a number the source did not give is left out or marked illustrative. One data module drives every figure so the numbers agree with each other.
- Check the science or the logic of each step before animating it; a beautiful wrong diagram is worse than none.
- End on the one idea in one line. No brand end card unless asked.

## Tells for this type

A slide of bullets; icons in circles; three cards in a row; the whole diagram at once; a narrator repeating the text on screen word for word.
# Story

Read before building any video that tells something over about 15 s: a launch or promo, an explainer, a pull-request or changelog video, a recap, a music video with a narrative. Most weak films are good motion around no story: a list of features, three cards in a row, a logo, a URL.

Skip it for an edit to an existing project, captions or overlays on footage, and a short single-idea piece (one kinetic line, a map move, a highlight on an image), where the request is the story. When the person gave a script, a storyboard or a reference film, follow theirs. The shape of each kind of film (launch, explainer, music, data, vertical, 3D, character) is in `types/`.

## 1. The one thing

- **What it is**, in one line: "You can now …" for a launch, the one idea the viewer must understand for an explainer, what changed and why it matters for a pull request. A whole release ("2.0", "what's new") is not one thing: take its headline.
- **The one thing to remember** after the film ends, in the viewer's words, not the brand slogan.
- **One viewer doing one real task**, from the moment they need it to the result. That task is the spine, and one real piece of data (a query, a file, a prompt, a number) travels through it from the hook to the payoff. An explainer's spine is one concrete example worked through.
- Keep facts (what it does, real numbers, real labels) apart from creative choices (angle, tone, look). Every claim on screen traces to the source: the site, the PR, the docs or the person's words. Use the person's own copy verbatim.
- What the source does not say stays unsaid: never derive a claim it did not make ("40 min to 2 min" is not "20× faster"), mark an example number as illustrative, and show a screen you cannot get as a labelled placeholder, not a drawn one.

## 2. Three storylines, then one

Write three. They are three different films, not three titles on one film: each has its own **world** (where it happens and what it looks like), its own **device** (what the story is) and its own **form** (how the camera and the cuts carry it). Sketch five or more ideas first, a line each pairing a device with a form (tables below); drop those the subject cannot carry well, and of the rest keep the three that differ most. # Audio engine — voiceover, music, SFX, captions, transcription

For a full audio pass (TTS voiceover + background music + sound effects in one
shot), use the shared engine at `audio/scripts/audio.mjs`. It takes a neutral
--
`.media/audio/{voice,bgm,sfx}`:

```bash
node <SKILL_DIR>/audio/scripts/audio.mjs --request ./audio_request.json --out ./audio_meta.json
--
- **Request** `{ provider?, voice?, lang?, speed?, tts_model?, style?, lines: [{ id, text, style?, sfx?: [names] }], bgm: { mode?, query?, prompt? } }`: `id` joins each line back to your model; `bgm.mode` = `retrieve | generate | none` (omit for auto). `--only tts,bgm,sfx` runs a subset and merges into an existing `--out`.
- **Gemini narration** is opt-in with `provider: "gemini"` and an API key or service-account credentials. `tts_model` defaults to `gemini-3.8-flash-tts`; 3.8 Flash-Lite, 3.1 Flash Preview, and 2.5 Pro/Flash Preview TTS are also supported. `style` directs delivery; a line's style overrides the request's style. CLI overrides: `--tts-model`, `--style`. See `audio/references/tts.md` for a complete request. The existing automatic provider order is unchanged.
- **Output** `audio_meta.json` (id-keyed): `voices[].{path,duration_s,words[]}` (word timestamps for captions), `sfx[]`, `bgm`, `total_duration_s`.
- **HeyGen free-usage path**: HeyGen CLI auth unlocks TTS plus music retrieval; SFX come from Openverse with no account (`audio/references/sfx.md`). Local/provider-specific generators are explicit alternatives where installed; run `npx hyperframes media-use resolve --doctor` before assuming retrieval or TTS will work.
- If BGM took the generate path (`bgm_pending: true`), run `audio/scripts/wait-bgm.mjs` before final render.

Single-shot helpers: `audio/scripts/heygen-tts.mjs` (one voice file). Transcription / background removal / captions use the `hyperframes` CLI (`transcribe`, `remove-background`), see the per-topic guides in `audio/references/` (`tts.md`, `bgm.md`, `sfx.md`, `transcribe.md`, `remove-background.md`, `captions/`).

Transcription defaults to Parakeet (better than whisper.cpp: 6.05% vs 7.44% WER, 5-10x faster) via `scripts/transcribe.mjs`, with whisper.cpp auto-fallback (see `references/operations.md`).

# Sound effects (SFX)

Named sound effects, produced by the shared audio engine (`scripts/audio.mjs` → `scripts/lib/sfx.mjs`). No account or key is needed:

- **Openverse first, per cue.** Each cue is searched on [Openverse](https://openverse.org)'s free audio API (most sound effects come from Freesound). Search-and-download, **not** generation.
- **The bundled 21-file library is the fallback** (`assets/sfx/` + `manifest.json`): a cue Openverse has no usable match for, and every cue once Openverse is offline or rate limited, is matched against it and the file copied into the project.

There is no `npx hyperframes sfx` command. SFX is never generated — it is retrieved from Openverse (online) or taken from the bundled library (offline). `npx hyperframes media-use resolve --type sfx` follows the same order (`--local-only` skips Openverse).

## Licences

Only **CC0** and **CC BY** sounds are used: never NonCommercial, ShareAlike or NoDerivatives. Each CC BY sound is credited in the project's `assets/sfx/CREDITS.md` (title, creator, licence, source link; for `resolve`, in a `CREDITS.md` beside the sound files it saves) and its `audio_meta.sfx[]` entry carries `license` and `credit`. Tell the person to include those credits wherever the video is published.

## Cues — request → meta

Each line names the effects it wants: `lines[].sfx: ["whoosh", "ui click"]`. The engine flattens these into cues, resolves each, dedupes identical `(id, name)` pairs (the same effect named twice downloads/copies once), and writes `audio_meta.sfx[]`:

```jsonc
{
  "id": "3",                       // joins the cue to the caller's model (frame / scene / segment)
  "name": "whoosh",
  "file": "assets/sfx/whoosh.mp3", // downloaded or copied, relative to project root
  "source": "openverse" | "local", // which route resolved it
  "offset_s": 0,                   // delay from the line's start
  "duration_s": 0.57,
  "volume": 0.35,                  // SFX sit UNDER voice + BGM
  "license": "by",                 // Openverse only: "cc0" or "by"
  "credit": "\"Swoosh\" by Ana is licensed under CC BY 4.0. …" // Openverse only
}
```

A cue that matches nothing is **skipped** (recorded as an anomaly); SFX never blocks a render. Neither route replaces a file of yours already at the output name: the cue gets the next free name (`whoosh-2.mp3`), reported as an anomaly, and `file` carries the real path.

## Openverse

One search per distinct effect name (20 results, `license=cc0,by`; each result's licence is checked again). The pick keeps Openverse's relevance order, prefers clips that fit a cue (15 s at most; past ~4 s ranks lower) and CC0 over CC BY when they are close. The file lands at `assets/sfx/<slug>.<ext>` and `duration_s` comes from the result. Name effects concretely (`glass shatter`, not `dramatic sound`); a vague query returns a poor match. Anonymous use allows 20 searches a minute and 200 a day: past that, the rest of the run uses the bundled library.

## Bundled library (fallback)

21 curated files in `assets/sfx/`, indexed by `manifest.json` — `{ file, duration, description }` per key (e.g. `whoosh`, `pop`, `click`, `chime`, `riser`, `impact-bass-1`, `glitch-1`, `typing`, …). A cue name resolves by **manifest key, file basename, or slug**, so `whoosh`, `whoosh.mp3`, or `"ui click"` (→ slug) all match. Matched files are copied into the project's `assets/sfx/`; `duration_s` comes from the manifest, so timing is known **offline** — e.g. `riser` is 10.03s, so trigger it at `climax − 10.03s`. The manifest's `description` field carries placement hints per effect; read `assets/sfx/manifest.json` for the full set and usage.

## Rules

- **Volume ~0.35.** SFX must sit under narration and BGM, not fight them.
- **No match → skip, don't fail.** A missing effect logs an anomaly and moves on; never a render blocker.
- **Retrieval (Openverse) or bundled library (offline) — never generation.**
- **One asset per distinct name.** Reuse across lines is deduped to a single search and download, many cues.
- **Credit CC BY sounds.** `CREDITS.md` lists them; keep it with the project.

# HyperFrames Composition Project

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

Compositions A composition is an HTML document that defines a video timeline. Structure Every composition needs a root element with data-composition-id:
Nested Compositions Embed one composition inside another:
Listing Compositions Use npx hyperframes compositions to see all compositions in a project. Variables Two attributes with different shapes and different jobs: • **data-composition-variables** on the root — a JSON **array of declarations** ({id, type, label, default} per entry). Defines the schema: which variables exist, what type they are, and what defaults to use when no override is provided. • **data-variable-values** on a sub-comp host element — a JSON **object keyed by variable id** ({"title":"Pro","price":"$29"}). Carries per-instance overrides for that one mount of the sub-composition. They aren't redundant — one is "what variables does this composition have?" and the other is "what values should this particular embed use?" Inside any composition script, window.__hyperframes.getVariables() returns the merged result. Layering, lowest to highest precedence: 1. Declared defaults from data-composition-variables 2. Per-instance overrides from the host's data-variable-values (sub-comp embeds only) 3. CLI overrides from npx hyperframes render --variables '{...}' (top-level renders only)

The runtime layers data-variable-values over the sub-comp's declared defaults on a per-instance basis. The same getVariables() call works at the top level too — the CLI flag --variables provides the override, declared defaults fall through for missing keys.

         数据库表 hotels（行可变脏、可回滚）、快照盘、题目卡、判分规则卡（JSON）、agent 光标

steps.text:
The video is done: 48 s, 1920×1080, 30 fps, no voiceover, just a few UI sound effects. `check` has no errors, and I looked at frames from every scene before rendering. I checked the sound with the audio tool but couldn't listen to it, and there's no music track because this machine has no music source.

The same hotel-site example runs through the whole video: the Booking replica at `localhost:8080`, the hotels table, and the question "在 Booking 上搜维也纳，筛四星以上，告诉我第一家酒店的名字和价格", whose answer is Hotel Kaiserhof Wien, €189.

| Time | Content |
|---|---|
| 0–4.5 s | Opening: the question card sits on the replica's search results. Title: "这样一道 Web Agent 题，怎么造、怎么判？" |
| 4.5–13.5 s | **① Replicate the site:** booking.com and the `localhost:8080` replica side by side. The replica's hotel cards build up one by one, and each matching row lands in the local `hotels` table at the same time. |
| 13.5–24 s | **② Reset data:** the previous question was "订 Kaiserhof 3 间房". `rooms_left` dropped to 0, a booking was added, and the page shows the hotel sold out, so the next question's answer would change. Then `reset → snapshot_v0` turns each field from red back to its green initial value. |
| 24–34 s | **③ Generate the question from data:** the city (Vienna, 97 hotels at 4★+) and the star level 4 are drawn from the hotels table, then filled into the `{city}` / `{n}` template slots. A check confirms the question has an answer, and the question is generated. Cycling the city to Paris, Tokyo and so on shows each change makes a new question. |
| 34–44 s | **④ Question + scoring rules:** the question and a JSON scoring rule appear together. The SQL query fills in the expected answer `('Hotel Kaiserhof Wien', 189)`. The agent's answer is compared field by field, gets a PASS stamp, and "让大模型打分" is struck out. |
| 44–48 s | Closing: "题目从数据里来，答案也从数据里来", followed by a one-line recap of the four steps. |

**Note:** the hotel names, counts (312 / 97) and prices are all made-up example data, not taken from the real site. Please don't present them as real results.

The browser chrome and card labels in the replica (URL bar, "每晚" and so on) use 18–24px type. `check` warns about this. I left it that size on purpose to look like a real web page. The main titles and the lines meant to be read are large and clear.

I also considered two other versions and didn't make them: one continuous camera shot moving through a single big diagram, and a before/after comparison of LLM scoring versus scoring against the database. The design choices are in `SPEC.md` and the review notes in `REVIEW.md`. The weakest part is step 4, which packs a lot onto one screen; with more time I'd split it into two parts.

To keep editing, run `npx hyperframes preview --background` to open the editing preview, or use the HyperFrames desktop app: https://hyperframes.dev/studio/download?os=linux
